pr_title: feat: Preserve base dtype when raising to `UInt` power
pr_body:
closes #9051 

~todo: fixup the return schema for the lazy case~
pr_comments:
@ritchie46 were you aware that this PR disallows raising a uint series to a negative integer which was previously allowed? I feel it should have been more clearly mentioned in the PR description/title/changelog.

See https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/15897

This issue bit me and was not trivial to debug when upgrading as I had some code like this:

```
priors = (
        pl.scan_ndjson(ndjson, infer_schema_length=10000)
        .select(
            [
                pl.col("nearestNodes"),
                pl.col("nearestNodes")
                .list.len()
                .pow(1).inspect()
                .alias("1/nearestNodesListLength"),
            ]
        )
        .inspect()
        .filter(pl.col("nearestNodes").list.len() > 0)
        .explode("nearestNodes")
        .group_by("nearestNodes")
        .sum()
        .sort("1/nearestNodesListLength", descending=True)
        .with_columns(
            [
                (
                    pl.col("1/nearestNodesListLength")
                    / pl.col("1/nearestNodesListLength").sum()
                ).alias("priors"),
            ]
        )
        .with_columns(
            [
                pl.col("priors").log10().alias("log_priors"),
            ]
        )
        .collect()
    )
```

suddenly giving a very unspecific error:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/opt/homebrew/Caskroom/miniforge/base/envs/py11/lib/python3.11/site-packages/polars/dataframe/frame.py", line 7701, in select
    return self.lazy().select(*exprs, **named_exprs).collect(_eager=True)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/opt/homebrew/Caskroom/miniforge/base/envs/py11/lib/python3.11/site-packages/polars/lazyframe/frame.py", line 1708, in collect
    return wrap_df(ldf.collect())
                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
polars.exceptions.ComputeError: conversion from `i32` to `u32` failed in column 'literal' for 1 out of 1 values: [-1]
```

The PR title only talks about raising to `UInt` power, when in fact it _also_ disallows raising to `Int` power.

The docs for pow have not been adjusted but should be: https://docs.pola.rs/docs/python/dev/reference/expressions/api/polars.Expr.pow.html

issue_context.title: `pow`: return `Int64` for `Int64` ** `Int64`, and raise if exponent is negative integer?
issue_context.body:
### Polars version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.


### Issue description

Currently, `pow` always returns `float` dtype

This came up here: https://github.com/data-apis/dataframe-api/issues/174

The Array API would return `int` for `int` to the power of `int`, and says that `int` to the power of something negative is implementation-dependent

One suggestion could be:
- `int_base_series.pow(int_exponent_series)` returns `int` dtype if `int_exponent_series` is all non-negative
- `int_base_series.pow(int_exponent_series)` raises if `int_exponent_series` contains negative numbers
- `float_base_series.pow(int_exponent_series)` returns `float` dtype
- `int_base_series.pow(float_exponent_series)` returns `float` dtype
- `float_base_series.pow(float_exponent_series)` returns `float` dtype

This is what pyarrow does:
```python

In [18]: pc.power(pa.array([1 ,2]), pa.array([1, 2]))
Out[18]:
<pyarrow.lib.Int64Array object at 0x7f75ea63d000>
[
  1,
  4
]

In [19]: pc.power(pa.array([1 ,2]), pa.array([-1, 2]))
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ArrowInvalid: integers to negative integer powers are not allowed

In [20]: pc.power(pa.array([1 ,2]), pa.array([-1., 2.]))
Out[20]:
<pyarrow.lib.DoubleArray object at 0x7f75ea6e8460>
[
  1,
  4
]

In [21]: pc.power(pa.array([1. ,2.]), pa.array([-1, 2]))
Out[21]:
<pyarrow.lib.DoubleArray object at 0x7f75ea31f760>
[
  1,
  4
]

In [22]: pc.power(pa.array([1. ,2.]), pa.array([-1., 2.]))
Out[22]:
<pyarrow.lib.DoubleArray object at 0x7f75ea6ebf40>
[
  1,
  4
]
```

### Reproducible example

```python
In [13]: pl.Series([1,2,3]).pow(pl.Series([1,2,3]))
Out[13]:
shape: (3,)
Series: '' [f64]
[
        1.0
        4.0
        27.0
]
```


### Expected behavior

```python
shape: (3,)
Series: '' [i64]
[
        1
        4
        27
]
```
, like `pyarrow`

---

Note: this already was raised [here ](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/4796), but it looks like there wasn't much discussion, so I'm bringing it up again, hope it's OK

comments: I feel integer power should have a separate function, and that the default power function should always return a float. I think it's rather poor design to change the type of the output column based on the value of the exponent. It can lead to subtle breakage where suddenly a column becomes integer and later on floats are expected.

isn't this what already happens for, say, multiplication though?

e.g. multiplying an int column by an integer returns an integer, but multiplying an int column by a float returns a float
```python
In [65]: pl.Series([1,2])*4
Out[65]:
shape: (2,)
Series: '' [i64]
[
        4
        8
]

In [66]: pl.Series([1,2])*4.
Out[66]:
shape: (2,)
Series: '' [f64]
[
        4.0
        8.0
]
```

The return type would still be predictable, based on the rules defined above

Sorry, coming back to this, I'm not too keen on

>  if int_exponent_series is all non-negative

. Such a condition wouldn't be predictable for lazy execution, right?

How about:

- `uint_base_series.pow(uint_exponent_series)` returns `uint` dtype
- `int_base_series.pow(uint_exponent_series)` returns `int` dtype
- `int_base_series.pow(int_exponent_series)` returns `float` dtype
- `float_base_series.pow(int_exponent_series)` returns `float` dtype
- `int_base_series.pow(float_exponent_series)` returns `float` dtype
- `float_base_series.pow(float_exponent_series)` returns `float` dtype
Yes output should be dependent on the schema, not on the data and same type arguments should produce the same type 👍
